findings.claim: Break-glass bypass gates 2 and 3 are mutually incompatible: verify-bypass-pairing.sh requires a rule_id field in the waiver entry, but the pre-existing schemas/waiver.schema.json has additionalProperties: false with no rule_id property, so gate 3 (JSON-schema validation) rejects any waiver document that gate 2 would accept.
findings.evidence: scripts/verify-bypass-pairing.sh lines 41-44: `jq -e --arg rule_id ... 'any(.[]?; .rule_id? == $rule_id)'` and line 46: grep for added `rule_id` key in diff — both require rule_id in the waiver entry. schemas/waiver.schema.json: required=[waiver_id,finding_id,reason,approved_by,expires_at,created_at], additionalProperties: false, properties list contains no rule_id. A waivers entry with rule_id fails schema validation (additional property not allowed); without rule_id fails the pairing script. The new policy-check-summary.schema.json waivers_applied field correctly models anyOf[rule_id, finding_id] but that is the summary output schema, not the bypass-gate input validation schema.
findings.impact: The three-gate break-glass model (AC viii-c) is permanently non-functional as committed. Every real scp_bypass=true invocation against a deny finding will emit SCP-E004 from one gate or the other regardless of waivers.json content. The governance procedure described in ADOPT-001 §12 break-glass section (not yet written, but scoped to 020H part 3) will document a procedure that cannot succeed. If 020E.a canary tests ever exercise scp_bypass=true, they will fail.
findings.mitigation: Option A (preferred, contained in scope): Replace the $ref in schemas/waivers-file.schema.json with an inline anyOf schema supporting two entry shapes — a rule-bypass shape (required: [rule_id, approved_by, expires_at, reason], optional finding_id) and a finding-waiver shape (required: [waiver_id, finding_id, reason, approved_by, expires_at, created_at]) — mirroring the intent of WP-SCP-020 §4 020C SCP-R-002 ('required keys approved_by, created_at, expires_at, rule_id OR finding_id'). This is an in-scope change to schemas/waivers-file.schema.json. Option B: defer to 020C by replacing the inline jsonschema validation in the bypass step with a plain Python check for required fields (approved_by, expires_at, rule_id) without a schema file, and note that full schema validation awaits the 020C SCP-R-002 rule. Either option must add a verify_command confirming the bypass gate accepts a synthetic rule_id entry and rejects a missing one.

findings.claim: The Conftest vendored-binary fallback path (vendor/conftest/conftest) is accepted and executed without SHA256 verification. A caller who commits a trojanised binary at that path can cause the workflow to execute an attacker-controlled Conftest binary that fabricates policy findings (e.g., returns all-allow), completely neutralising policy enforcement.
findings.evidence: resolve_conftest() at policy-check.yml lines 128-145 has three resolution paths: (1) download+SHA256 verify, (2) vendored archive+SHA256 verify, (3) plain vendored binary vendor/conftest/conftest with no integrity check whatsoever (lines 140-142: 'if [ -f "${vendored_binary}" ]; then printf "%s\n" "${vendored_binary}"; return 0; fi'). By contrast OPA receives gh attestation verify after SHA256 (line 151). Conftest has no Sigstore attestation call at all. Any commit that places a file at vendor/conftest/conftest bypasses both SHA256 and Sigstore verification and is executed as the policy engine. The Conftest binary produces the policy-findings.json that all downstream steps â threshold enforcement, bypass gate, conflict gate, summary artefact â depend on for correctness.
findings.impact: A caller repo (or a compromised Codex dispatch during 020C or later) that commits vendor/conftest/conftest with a malicious binary causes every policy check run in that repo to return a fabricated verdict. The binary can emit all-allow findings, suppressing every SCP-R-NNN deny. The SHA256 hash hardcoded in the workflow matches the legitimate Conftest release, so the lack of verification on the vendor binary path is invisible in the workflow YAML. The required check (scp/policy-check) passes. All downstream estate repos that adopt this workflow inherit the same vulnerability if they commit a vendor/ directory. This undermines the entire security invariant of 020B.
findings.mitigation: Remove the plain-binary vendor fallback (lines 140-142). The two safe fallback paths (download+SHA256 and vendored-archive+SHA256) are sufficient. If an offline vendor binary is needed, require it to be the .tar.gz archive with verified SHA256 â never a bare executable. Additionally add gh attestation verify for Conftest once Conftest publishes Sigstore attestations (track at open-policy-agent/conftest); until then add a compensating comment in the workflow explaining why Sigstore is absent and that the bare-binary vendor path is disabled.

findings.claim: actionlint (or equivalent workflow-syntax linter) is absent from the dispatch-package verify_commands, violating WP-SCP-022 §4.1's mandatory requirement for workflow slices.
findings.evidence: WP-SCP-022 §4.1: 'for workflow slices includes actionlint (or workflow-syntax linter)'. dispatch-package.json verify_commands contains: test -f, test -x, test -f, python3 additionalProperties check, bash -n (shell syntax), python3 yaml.safe_load + permissions/secrets check, python3 regex check for run: interpolation. No actionlint invocation is present.
findings.impact: GitHub Actions-specific syntax errors (unknown action inputs, invalid context expression types, job-level field misuse) that pass bash -n and yaml.safe_load will not be caught at verify time. Downstream 020B.1 integration tests assume the workflow is syntactically valid for GitHub Actions; a latent Actions-syntax error discovered in 020B.1 requires an out-of-sequence fix round on an already-merged slice.
findings.mitigation: Add `actionlint .github/workflows/policy-check.yml` to verify_commands in the dispatch-package and re-run verify. If actionlint is not pre-installed in the execution environment, add a tool-version pin to scripts/.tool-versions (per 020B.2 scope) or use `pip install actionlint-py` inline. This is a required field per §4.1 for all workflow slices and cannot be waived.

findings.claim: The plan's criterion (xi) claims the commit-status context will be exactly scp/policy-check, but GitHub Actions reusable-workflow behaviour produces a combined {calling-job-name} / scp/policy-check context string; no documentation in the slice guides 020D1/020D2 on the required calling-job configuration to produce this exact string.
findings.evidence: Workflow line 42: `name: scp/policy-check` (callee job name set correctly). GitHub Actions documentation: 'When you use a reusable workflow, the check name is made up of the calling workflow job name and the reusable workflow job name, concatenated with a forward slash.' The 020H part 3 minimal wrapper example in WP-SCP-020 §4 uses job key `policy-check` with no explicit name, which would produce context `policy-check / scp/policy-check`, not `scp/policy-check`. No comment in the workflow or note in the dispatch-package addresses this.
findings.impact: When 020D2 configures the required status check on SCP main using the string scp/policy-check (per the plan's invariant and the criterion statement), the branch-protection rule will never match any real check and will permanently display 'Expected — Waiting'. The entire purpose of 020D2 is defeated, and WP-SCP-023's aggregator consumer will be misconfigured. The correct context string to use in branch protection depends on what name the 020D1 caller job uses, which is currently undocumented.
findings.mitigation: Add a comment to the workflow's job definition and/or the dispatch-package notes field stating: 'Branch-protection required-status-check context for this job is {calling-job-name} / scp/policy-check. To resolve to exactly scp/policy-check, the 020D1 caller wrapper must set its job name appropriately (e.g. empty name with job key scp-policy-check) or branch-protection must be configured with the actual combined context. Verify empirically in 020E.a what context GitHub shows for the caller+callee combination before 020D2 configures branch protection.' Alternatively, the plan criterion can be clarified in the 020D2 dispatch-package to use the verified combined context string.

findings.claim: `schemas/waivers-file.schema.json` is referenced in the bypass-gate step but never committed, making AC (viii-c) gate-3 unexercisable after 020C lands Rego rules.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 270: `schema_path = Path("schemas/waivers-file.schema.json")`. File absent from repo and from dispatch-package.json `scope_boundary`. The `except Exception` at line 274 catches `FileNotFoundError` and emits `SCP-E004::waiver schema validation failed: [Errno 2] No such file...` — a misleading message. In 020B's scaffold the bypass path short-circuits at the empty-findings check (line 243), so the missing file is currently invisible; it materialises as a silent hard failure as soon as 020C produces a deny finding.
findings.impact: With `scp_bypass: true` on a post-020C PR that has a genuine deny finding, the workflow passes gates 1 and 2, then fails gate 3 with an opaque error that looks like a schema-content failure rather than a missing artefact. No bypass path can ever succeed until the file is committed. Operators have no clean failure signal to diagnose this.
findings.mitigation: Commit a minimal `schemas/waivers-file.schema.json` (JSON Schema draft 2020-12, `additionalProperties: false`, required fields `rule_id|finding_id`, `approved_by`, `created_at`, `expires_at`) as part of slice 020B or annotate the workflow with an `# FIXME: requires schemas/waivers-file.schema.json from 020C.1` comment and a guard that emits `SCP-E001` + advisory message when the file is missing, rather than silently failing via the generic exception handler.

findings.claim: The commit-status context that GitHub will record for this `workflow_call` job is NOT guaranteed to be `scp/policy-check` as criterion (xi) requires, because the check name is determined by the calling workflow's job-name configuration, not by the reusable workflow's own `name:` or job `name:` fields.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 1: `name: policy-check`; line 42: `name: scp/policy-check`. For `workflow_call` reusable workflows, GitHub creates a check run whose context (the string that branch protection's `required_status_checks.contexts[]` must match) is formed from the calling workflow's job name, not the reusable workflow's job name. The 020H part-3 example caller stub (WP-SCP-020 §4 020H part 3) names its job `policy-check`, which would produce a check context of `policy-check / scp/policy-check` or just `policy-check`—neither of which equals `scp/policy-check`. The plan requires `scp/policy-check` for WP-SCP-023 aggregation and 020D2 branch-protection configuration.
findings.impact: If 020D2 configures branch protection with `required_status_checks.contexts: ["scp/policy-check"]` and the actual check name is different (e.g., `policy-check / scp/policy-check`), the required check is never satisfied and the gate is either permanently failing or permanently skipped. The entire enforcement model depends on this name being correct.
findings.mitigation: Empirically verify the check name during 020E.a (pre-protection canary): run `gh pr view <PR> --json statusCheckRollup` after the reusable workflow completes and record the exact `context` string. If the actual context differs from `scp/policy-check`, update the dispatch-package for 020D2 with the verified name and amend criterion (xi) in WP-SCP-020 with a note on the required caller job-name convention. As a defence, document in the ADOPT-001 §12 wrapper template that the calling job MUST be named such that the combined check context resolves to `scp/policy-check`.

findings.claim: The generated `policy-check-summary.json` is uploaded as an artifact without being validated against `schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json`, so schema-invalid summaries are silently accepted.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 362-398 build the summary; lines 400-406 upload it. No step calls `jsonschema.validate` (or any other validator) against `schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json`. Critically, `pr_sha` is set to `os.environ.get("SCP_PR_SHA", "")` (line 386); the schema at schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json line 24-27 requires `"pattern": "^[0-9a-f]{40}$"`. An empty-string default produces a schema-invalid artifact that uploads without any error. Similarly, `base_ref` and `rule_set` have `minLength: 1`; empty defaults would silently violate those constraints.
findings.impact: WP-SCP-023 and any downstream consumer that validates the summary artifact before ingesting it will fail silently or crash on a schema-invalid document. The schema commitment is meaningless if it is never enforced at production time.
findings.mitigation: Add a validation step between 'Build policy-check summary' and 'Upload policy-check summary artifact': `python3 -c "import json, jsonschema; jsonschema.validate(json.load(open('policy-check-summary.json')), json.load(open('schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json')))"`. Emit `SCP-E001` and exit 1 on validation failure. Also guard `pr_sha` production: if `SCP_PR_SHA` is not a 40-char hex string, emit `SCP-E001` and exit 1 before writing the file, so the artifact is never uploaded in an invalid state.

findings.claim: verify-bypass-pairing.sh validates that waivers.json contains the bypass rule_id and that the entry appears as an added diff line, but never checks that expires_at is in the future. An expired waiver â or a waiver with expires_at: '2021-01-01' â fully satisfies the bypass gate.
findings.evidence: Script lines 41-48: jq checks rule_id presence; grep -E checks the entry appears as a new '+' line in the diff. Neither check reads or compares expires_at against the current date. schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json defines expires_at (line 101, line 128) as 'type: string, minLength: 1' â no format constraint, no minimum-date constraint. The Python schema validation step (workflow lines 259-277) validates against schemas/waivers-file.schema.json which is not part of the 020B scope boundary and whose expires_at constraints are unknown; even if waivers-file.schema.json enforces ISO-8601 format, it does not compare the value to now(). The bypass gate is therefore satisfiable by adding a waiver entry that expired years ago.
findings.impact: An operator who legitimately obtained a waiver in the past (or a malicious adopter who pre-dates a waiver) can reuse an expired waiver to unlock the break-glass bypass. The waivers.json diff-membership check is satisfied (the expired waiver is added as a new line), the rule_id matches, the schema validates, and the bypass gate exits 0 â all while the waiver's authorisation window is long closed. The time-bounded nature of the waiver (the core governance control) is unenforced.
findings.mitigation: Add an expires_at validation step in verify-bypass-pairing.sh after the jq check: extract expires_at for the matching rule_id entry and compare it to the current UTC date using date -d and/or python3 -c. Fail with SCP-E004 if expires_at <= today. Also add 'format: date' and a pattern constraint ('^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$') to expires_at in schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json for both disabled_rules and waivers_applied entries; this ensures downstream consumers (WP-SCP-023 aggregators) can parse dates reliably.

findings.claim: verify-bypass-pairing.sh verifies that a D-NNN row was added to docs/DECISIONS.md but does not verify that the row references the bypass rule_id. A PR can add any unrelated D-NNN row (e.g., a legitimate architecture decision) to satisfy the governance gate while the waivers.json entry covers the actual bypass â the documentation trail is decoupled from the technical event.
findings.evidence: Script line 31: 'git diff --unified=0 ... -- docs/DECISIONS.md | grep -Eq '^\+\|\s*D-0[0-9]{3}\s*\|\s*20[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}\s*\|'' â the regex checks that some D-NNN table row was added. It does not grep for the specific rule_id (BYPASS_RULE_ID=$1), nor does it require any field in the row to contain the bypassed rule. The plan AC (viii-c)(2) states 'a sibling commit in the same PR contains both a docs/DECISIONS.md D-NNN record AND a matching waivers.json entry' â the intent is clear linkage, but the script does not enforce it. A PR that adds D-031 (some unrelated infra decision) and a waivers.json entry for SCP-R-001 satisfies both checks without the D-031 row mentioning SCP-R-001 at all.
findings.impact: The governance documentation trail for a break-glass event may be an unrelated D-NNN row that gives no indication a policy bypass occurred. Audit consumers (WP-SCP-023, future human auditors) who review DECISIONS.md for bypass evidence will not find it unless they also correlate waivers-applied records. The governance invariant that bypass events are traceable in DECISIONS.md is formally satisfied but semantically empty.
findings.mitigation: Extend the DECISIONS.md grep to also require the bypass rule_id to appear in the same added table row: after confirming the D-NNN row exists, run a second grep that combines both patterns, e.g., git diff ... -- docs/DECISIONS.md | grep -E '^\+.*D-0[0-9]{3}' | grep -Fq "${rule_id}". This ensures the specific row added references the rule being bypassed. Additionally, document in the AC that the D-NNN row's description column must name the bypassed rule_id â the script can enforce presence, human review of the row content is the second control.

findings.claim: verify-bypass-pairing.sh line 46 interpolates the unescaped rule_id argument directly into a grep -E extended-regex pattern. A rule_id containing regex metacharacters changes the matching semantics; a rule_id of '.*' makes the grep match any line in the waivers diff that contains 'rule_id', bypassing the requirement that the specific rule appears as a newly-added entry.
findings.evidence: Script line 46: 'grep -Eq "^\+.*\"rule_id\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"${rule_id}\""'. The ${rule_id} is interpolated unescaped into the -E regex. Metacharacters .+?*|[]{}() in rule_id alter pattern semantics. Example: rule_id='.*' â pattern '^\+.*"rule_id":".*"' which matches any added line containing 'rule_id' followed by any value â not just the target rule. Example: rule_id='SCP-R-001|SCP-R-002' â pattern becomes an alternation matching either rule. The BYPASS_RULE_ID is extracted from policy-findings.json via Python print() (workflow line 241) without sanitisation; if the policy evaluation (020C) is manipulated to produce a finding with a crafted rule_id, the regex is attacker-influenced. The jq call at line 41 correctly uses --arg rule_id (jq-safe), but the grep at line 46 does not.
findings.impact: With a manipulated policy evaluation producing a finding whose rule_id is '.*', the diff-membership check at line 46 accepts any waivers.json diff that contains any 'rule_id' key â not necessarily one matching the bypass rule. Combined with MAJ-BYPASS-003 (DECISIONS.md row not linked to rule_id), an attacker who can influence the policy output rule_id has full control over both bypass checks. The attack path requires compromising the policy evaluation step (020C scope), but the flaw in the script is present in 020B and will be live when 020C ships.
findings.mitigation: Use fgrep (grep -F, fixed-string match) instead of grep -E for the rule_id portion, or escape the rule_id before interpolation using printf '%s' "${rule_id}" | sed 's/[.^$*+?()[{|\\]/\\&/g'. Better: rewrite the diff check using jq for consistent semantics â pipe the waivers diff through jq to extract added rule_id values and compare literally: git diff ... -- "${waivers_path}" | grep '^+' | jq -Rs 'split("\n") | map(select(startswith("+"))) | ...' | jq -e --arg rid "${rule_id}" 'any(.[]; . == $rid)'. This eliminates regex injection entirely.

findings.claim: The 'Enforce break-glass pairing gates' step (if: inputs.scp_bypass) validates all three gates successfully but provides no mechanism to suppress the 'Render deny annotations and enforce threshold' step that unconditionally exits non-zero on deny findings. Break-glass is therefore operationally dead: a PR that satisfies all three gates still fails the required check, pushing operators toward disabling branch protection directly â a far more dangerous and unaudited bypass path.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml: the bypass gate step at line 211 has condition 'if: inputs.scp_bypass'. If all three gates pass, the step exits 0 with no output variable or env-write that signals bypass approval. The 'Render deny annotations and enforce threshold' step at lines 301-336 has no 'if:' condition and always runs. Python at line 334: 'if denies and os.environ.get("SCP_THRESHOLD") == "deny": sys.exit(1)' â SCP_BYPASS ('true') is never consulted. So a PR with scp_bypass=true that satisfies DECISIONS.md+waivers.json+schema produces: bypass gate exit 0, then threshold step exit 1, overall workflow exit 1, required check fails, merge blocked. Additionally: the bypass gate at lines 230-247 extracts BYPASS_RULE_ID from policy-findings.json and exits 1 if no deny finding exists â so scp_bypass=true with no deny findings also fails (the workflow fails when it would otherwise pass). The bypass input has no functional effect on any code path.
findings.impact: Any operator who follows the documented three-gate break-glass procedure and sets scp_bypass=true will see their PR fail anyway. Faced with a blocked emergency, they will likely: (a) ask to have the required check temporarily removed from branch protection, (b) push directly to main with admin override, or (c) create a dummy commit that forces the deny finding away. Options (a) and (b) are unaudited, don't produce the DECISIONS.md+waivers.json trail the system was designed to require, and leave no evidence in the policy artefacts. The break-glass design is sophisticated but the implementation makes it impossible to exercise â operators encounter a worse safety profile than if the bypass had never been designed.
findings.mitigation: After the bypass gate exits 0, write a step output or environment variable (e.g., echo 'SCP_BYPASS_APPROVED=true' >> $GITHUB_ENV). In the 'Render deny annotations and enforce threshold' step, check: 'if denies and os.environ.get("SCP_THRESHOLD") == "deny" and os.environ.get("SCP_BYPASS_APPROVED") != "true": sys.exit(1)'. This makes the threshold step respect a validated bypass. Additionally, emit a structured SCP-E004 annotation (already required by AC viii-b) only when the bypass is activated, to make bypass events visible in the PR timeline. Consider a dedicated summary line in the workflow summary stating 'BREAK-GLASS BYPASS ACTIVE â rule_id, expires_at, D-NNN ref' for audit visibility.

findings.claim: dispatch-package timeout_seconds of 2400 deviates from the WP-SCP-022 §4.1 default of 1800 for non-kernel-dangerous slices with no documented justification.
findings.evidence: dispatch-package.json: `"timeout_seconds": 2400`. WP-SCP-022 §4.1: 'timeout_seconds — default 1800 (30 min); kernel-dangerous slices (020J tag-protection) use 3600.' Slice 020B is not kernel-dangerous. The notes field does not explain the deviation.
findings.impact: No operational impact for this slice. Undocumented protocol deviations accumulate and erode confidence that §4.1 defaults are being honoured; future reviewers cannot distinguish an intentional exception from accidental inflation.
findings.mitigation: Either revert to 1800 if the extra 10 minutes provides no measured benefit, or add a brief rationale to the notes field: 'timeout raised to 2400s — binary download + SHA256 verification on cold GitHub-hosted runners can take 8–10 min; 1800 is borderline given two-binary resolution with network fallback.'

findings.claim: AC (viii-c) names the authorising workflow step `bypass-gate` but the implementing step is named 'Enforce break-glass pairing gates' with no explicit `id:` field.
findings.evidence: WP-SCP-020 §4 020B (viii-c): 'verified by `scripts/verify-bypass-pairing.sh` run in workflow step `bypass-gate`'. policy-check.yml line 210: `name: Enforce break-glass pairing gates`; no `id:` key on this step.
findings.impact: Tools or documentation that reference the step by `id: bypass-gate` (e.g., future workflow tooling, step-outcome checks, or the 020B.1 selftest harness) will fail to resolve the step. The plan's canonical name for the step is also inconsistent with the implementation.
findings.mitigation: Add `id: bypass-gate` to the step at line 210, or update the plan's reference in (viii-c) to match the chosen id slug. Prefer adding `id: bypass-gate` to the YAML.

findings.claim: `changed-files.txt` is written at line 180 but no subsequent step in the 020B scaffold reads it, leaving an undocumented dependency for 020C implementors.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 180: `git diff --name-only "${SCP_BASE_SHA}..${SCP_HEAD_SHA}" > changed-files.txt`. No other step references `changed-files.txt`. The 'Prepare workflow scaffold outputs' step (line 184) does not consume it.
findings.impact: 020C implementors who need to pass the changed-file list to Conftest/OPA must discover this implicit contract by reading the scaffold code; there is no comment, env-var, or output declaration advertising the file's purpose. A 020C dispatch that independently re-runs `git diff` would be silently redundant, and a 020C dispatch that misnames the file would silently miss files.
findings.mitigation: Add a comment to the 'Collect changed files' step: `# Output: changed-files.txt — consumed by the OPA/Conftest evaluation step added in slice 020C`. Alternatively, export the path as a step output (`echo "changed_files=changed-files.txt" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`) so 020C can reference it via `steps.collect-changed-files.outputs.changed_files`.

findings.claim: `rule_id` is interpolated directly into an extended-regex grep pattern in `verify-bypass-pairing.sh` without escaping, enabling regex-special characters in a rule_id to produce false matches or missed matches.
findings.evidence: verify-bypass-pairing.sh line 46: `grep -Eq "^\+.*\"rule_id\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"${rule_id}\""`. For `SCP-R-001` the `-` is safe outside a bracket expression, but a rule_id containing `.`, `*`, `+`, `(`, `)`, `\`, or `|` would expand as regex metacharacters. `rule_id` originates from `output/findings/policy-findings.json` which is workflow-controlled, but the sanitization chain between Rego output and this script is not documented.
findings.impact: A rule_id like `SCP-R-0.*` could match any waivers.json added line containing `rule_id`, producing a false-pass. Conversely, a rule_id with literal parentheses would cause the grep pattern to fail to compile, exiting non-zero and blocking the bypass.
findings.mitigation: Use `jq` for the waivers diff check instead of grep, consistent with line 41: `if ! git diff --unified=20 "${base_ref}..${head_ref}" -- "${waivers_path}" | python3 -c "import sys, json; diff=sys.stdin.read(); ..."`. Alternatively, use `grep -F` (fixed-string) for the outer match and layer the exact `rule_id` check via `jq` only, matching what line 41 already does.

findings.claim: The threshold check at line 334 does not inspect `SCP_BYPASS`, meaning the workflow exits 1 on deny findings even when the bypass gate has passed, and the bypass path's success depends entirely on 020C.1 waiver-aware Rego suppressing the deny upstream — a dependency not documented in-workflow.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 334: `if denies and os.environ.get("SCP_THRESHOLD") == "deny": sys.exit(1)`. `SCP_BYPASS` is available in the environment (set at line 48) but is not checked here. The only way the bypass path succeeds is if 020C.1's waiver-aware Rego converts the deny finding to a waived verdict before this step runs, resulting in `denies` being empty. This coupling is not noted in the scaffold.
findings.impact: A developer testing the bypass path before 020C.1 lands (e.g., by manually injecting a deny finding) will observe that even after passing all three bypass gates, the workflow still fails at the threshold check. This is surprising and will cause confusion during 020B.1 selftest harness development (the next slice), which may try to exercise the bypass path.
findings.mitigation: Add a comment above the threshold check: `# NOTE: bypass path succeeds only when 020C.1 waiver-aware Rego suppresses the deny finding upstream; SCP_BYPASS does not short-circuit this check by design.` This makes the architectural dependency explicit. Optionally, also add a log line when `SCP_BYPASS == true` and denies are non-empty: `print(f"::warning ::scp_bypass=true but {len(denies)} deny finding(s) remain un-waived; workflow will still fail")` to give operators an actionable signal.

findings.claim: schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json defines expires_at in both disabled_rules and waivers_applied as 'type: string, minLength: 1' with no format or pattern constraint. Any non-empty string passes schema validation. Downstream aggregators (WP-SCP-023) and the bypass gate's own schema validation will silently accept 'never', 'TBD', or '9999-99-99' as expires_at values.
findings.evidence: schema lines 99-103 (disabled_rules expires_at): 'type: string, minLength: 1'. Schema lines 128-130 (waivers_applied expires_at): identical. No 'format: date', no pattern '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$', no 'minimum' constraint. The Python schema validation in the bypass gate (workflow lines 259-277) validates waivers.json against schemas/waivers-file.schema.json, not this schema â but waivers-file.schema.json's expires_at constraints are outside the 020B scope boundary. The policy-check-summary.schema.json is the canonical consumer-facing schema per AC (x); its laxity sets the contract for all downstream processors.
findings.impact: WP-SCP-023 estate aggregators will receive summary artefacts with unparseable or semantically invalid expires_at values without schema-level rejection. A disabled rule with expires_at: 'indefinite' passes the schema, making the expiry field meaningless for automated tracking. The bypass-validity tracking (which depends on expires_at > today) becomes unreliable at the summary-artefact level. This is a MIN because the immediate gate check (in 020C.1) will be in the Rego waiver-aware logic, not the summary schema, but it establishes a bad contract.
findings.mitigation: Add 'format: date' and pattern '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$' to all expires_at fields in schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json. Add the same constraints to schemas/waivers-file.schema.json if it exists. Enable JSON Schema format validation (the default jsonschema library requires format_checker=jsonschema.FormatChecker() to enforce format keywords) in the Python validation step.

findings.claim: The 'Collect changed files' step (policy-check.yml line 180) runs 'git diff --name-only SCP_BASE_SHA..SCP_HEAD_SHA' without error-code emission. If SCP_BASE_SHA is absent from the local git history (force-push deleted the base branch history; workflow triggered outside pull_request context; unusual merge-base scenarios), the git diff exits non-zero due to set -euo pipefail but emits no SCP-E001 annotation â an infra failure is indistinguishable from a policy deny in the PR UI.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 163-181: the 'Collect changed files' step emits a structured SCP-E001 error for missing SCP_BASE_SHA/SCP_HEAD_SHA env vars (lines 175-178) but not for a git-diff failure on a present-but-unreachable SHA. The git diff at line 180 runs directly without a surrounding 'emit_infra_failure' wrapper. The checkout step uses fetch-depth: 0 (full history) which mitigates most shallow-clone scenarios, but force-push to the base branch between PR open and workflow run can still cause the base SHA to be garbage-collected or missing. The step exits with git's exit code, which the workflow surfaces as a generic step failure without an SCP-EXXX title.
findings.impact: Operators see a failing required check with no SCP-E001 annotation. They cannot distinguish a git infrastructure failure (retry/contact owner) from a genuine policy deny (fix code). Workflow log inspection is required to identify the root cause. This is MIN severity because the PR is correctly blocked (merge-blocked is the safe outcome) but the error UX violates AC (viii-b) which mandates named error codes for infra failures.
findings.mitigation: Wrap the git diff call at line 180 in a subshell with explicit error handling: 'git diff --name-only "${SCP_BASE_SHA}..${SCP_HEAD_SHA}" > changed-files.txt || emit_infra_failure "git diff failed: base SHA ${SCP_BASE_SHA} may not exist in local history (force-push or non-PR context)"'. The emit_infra_failure function already exists in this step's scope (defined at lines 168-172) and emits SCP-E001 before exiting.

findings.claim: The implementation commit message cites WP-SCP-022 (the programme plan) but not WP-SCP-020 §4 (the governing specification), slightly reducing bidirectional commit-history traceability.
findings.evidence: Git log: '0a415c9 WP-SCP-022 slice 020B: reusable policy-check workflow scaffold'. The governing spec is docs/plans/WP-SCP-020-policy-federation-primitive.md §4. dispatch-package.json spec_paths compensates in the evidence record.
findings.impact: Trivial. A reviewer grepping commit history for WP-SCP-020 will not find this commit directly. The dispatch-package.json spec_paths and the evidence directory provide adequate compensation.
findings.mitigation: Optionally add 'per WP-SCP-020 §4 020B' to the commit body. Not required to unblock the fix round.

findings.claim: OPA and Conftest are downloaded, SHA256-verified, and added to PATH in every workflow run, but no step in the 020B scaffold invokes them.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 64-161: full install step adds binaries to `$GITHUB_PATH`. Lines 162-406: no subsequent step calls `opa` or `conftest`. Approximately 15-30s of install overhead per PR run with no policy output.
findings.impact: Minor CI cost increase on every PR touching the repo until 020C wires up the evaluation step. No correctness impact.
findings.mitigation: No change required if the intent is to validate the install script itself as part of the scaffold. If the install overhead is a concern, gate the install step with `if: false` and a TODO comment referencing 020C, then remove the gate in the 020C dispatch.

findings.claim: The waivers-path existence check at lines 254-257 is dead code: `verify-bypass-pairing.sh` already checks and exits non-zero if `${waivers_path}` does not exist (line 36-39 of the script), so the outer check at 254-257 can never be reached if the file is absent.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 249-252: script is called; on exit-non-zero, `emit_error SCP-E004` fires and `exit 1` halts the step. Lines 254-257: `if [ ! -f "${SCP_WAIVERS_PATH}" ]; then emit_error SCP-E004 ...; exit 1; fi`. verify-bypass-pairing.sh lines 36-39: `if [ ! -f "${waivers_path}" ]; then echo "${waivers_path} does not exist" >&2; exit 1; fi`.
findings.impact: No runtime impact; the dead check adds noise and could mislead a reader into thinking the outer check is the primary guard.
findings.mitigation: Remove lines 254-257 from the bypass gate step, or move the existence check before the script invocation (so failures give a cleaner error message) and remove the duplicate inside the script.

findings.claim: verify-bypass-pairing.sh uses grep -Fxq (fixed-string exact-line match) to check whether waivers_path appears in the git diff output. The git diff --name-only output always omits the leading './' prefix. A caller who passes waivers-path: ./output/findings/waivers.json (note leading ./) will fail the diff-membership check even when the file was correctly modified in the PR, because './output/findings/waivers.json' != 'output/findings/waivers.json'.
findings.evidence: Script line 26: 'grep -Fxq "${waivers_path}" <<<"${changed_files}"'. The changed_files variable is populated by 'git diff --name-only base..HEAD' which emits paths as 'output/findings/waivers.json' (no leading './'). The waivers_path variable is set from SCP_WAIVERS_PATH which comes from the workflow input 'waivers-path'. The default value in the workflow ('output/findings/waivers.json') has no leading './' and works correctly. But the input description does not prohibit './output/findings/waivers.json', which a reasonable caller might supply. The -Fx flag means the mismatch silently causes a confusing SCP-E004 failure: 'output/findings/waivers.json must be part of the bypass diff' even though the file is visibly in the diff.
findings.impact: Minimal â the operator adjusts their caller wrapper. But the error message says the file is not in the diff when it actually is, creating a misleading debugging experience. Nit severity because the default value works and the AC does not require './' support.
findings.mitigation: Normalise waivers_path before the grep: 'waivers_path="${waivers_path#./}"' (strip leading './' if present). One line, no dependencies.
